primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'grace' (Greek: charis) primarily denotes God's unmerited, undeserved favor toward sinners — divine love and salvation freely given as a gift rather than earned by human works or merit, supremely expressed in Jesus Christ. It is the standard shorthand for the free, saving kindness of God that justifies, forgives, and reconciles humanity apart from any human deserving.
primary_basis: Ephesians 2:8-9 ('For by grace you have been saved through faith... not a result of works')
Romans 3:23-24 ('justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus')
Romans 5:15-21 (grace abounding through the one man Jesus Christ)
Romans 6:14 ('you are not under law but under grace')
Romans 11:6 ('if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works')
John 1:14-17 ('full of grace and truth... grace upon grace; the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ')
Titus 2:11 ('the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people')
2 Corinthians 8:9 ('you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor')
2 Timothy 1:9 (saved 'not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace')

alternatives.meaning: Grace as divine empowerment or enabling power — God's active strength working in and through believers to sustain them, equip them for ministry, and enable obedience, not merely a disposition of favor.
basis: 2 Corinthians 12:9 ('My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness')
1 Corinthians 15:10 ('by the grace of God I am what I am... I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me')
Hebrews 4:16 ('grace to help in time of need')

alternatives.meaning: Roman Catholic sacramental-theological reading: grace as an infused, created participation in the divine life (sanctifying/habitual grace) communicated especially through the sacraments, which actually transforms and elevates the soul rather than being only a favorable divine attitude.
basis: Romans 5:5 (love of God 'poured into our hearts')
Council of Trent's decree on justification as the classic doctrinal articulation

alternatives.meaning: Eastern Orthodox reading: grace as the uncreated energies of God himself — God's own presence and activity in which humans participate (theosis), following Gregory Palamas; grace is not a created gift or mere favor but God's self-communication.
basis: Exodus 33-34 and Transfiguration narratives (Matthew 17) as read in Palamite tradition

alternatives.meaning: Scholarly gift/benefaction reading: charis understood within Greco-Roman patronage conventions as 'gift' — incongruous (given without regard to worth) yet expecting a return of gratitude, loyalty, and transformed life; associated notably with John Barclay's 'Paul and the Gift,' which distinguishes multiple 'perfections' of grace rather than one meaning of 'unconditional favor.'
basis: 2 Corinthians 8-9 (charis used of the collection and of Christ's self-giving)
Comparative study of Second Temple Judaism and Greco-Roman benefaction texts

alternatives.meaning: Distinctions within Reformed and Wesleyan systems treating grace as differentiated categories — common grace (God's non-saving kindness to all creation, e.g., Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17), prevenient grace (grace that goes before and enables a free response, in Wesleyan/Arminian theology), and irresistible/efficacious grace (Calvinist soteriology). These are refinements of the primary meaning rather than rivals to it.

notes: Grace is one of the most stable and widely agreed theological terms in Christianity. Virtually all traditions converge on the core sense of 'unmerited divine favor,' often popularized by the acronym 'God's Riches At Christ's Expense' or the definition 'getting what we do not deserve.' The genuine divergences concern the mode and mechanics of grace (favorable attitude vs. infused quality vs. uncreated energy vs. reciprocal gift), and the extent/resistibility of grace (Catholic-Protestant, Calvinist-Arminian debates), not the basic symbolic meaning. The Hebrew background terms chen (favor, e.g., Genesis 6:8, 'Noah found grace/favor in the eyes of the LORD') and chesed (steadfast covenant love) are standardly cited as Old Testament roots of the concept.
